scenes.title: The File
scenes.summary: A dark room. Agent Fox enters, a folder lands on the desk, and the title appears.
scenes.narration: In 1977, the United States Senate held a hearing about a secret CIA program. Most of its files had been destroyed years earlier. But not all of them. The program was called MKUltra. So what was it? And how do we know?

en.text: So what was it? And how do we even know?

scenes.title: The Record
scenes.summary: Agent Fox examines declassified paperwork while a vintage map and archive labels drift behind him.
scenes.narration: Let's start with what the CIA itself told the Senate. According to the CIA director's testimony, MKUltra ran from 1953 to 1964. That's eleven years. The surviving records list 149 subprojects. They name 80 institutions, and 44 of them were colleges and universities. They also name 185 researchers and assistants from outside the government.

en.label: OUTSIDE RESEARCHERS & ASSISTANTS
en.note: Not government. Named right there in the records.

scenes.title: The Experiments
scenes.summary: A laboratory sketch: a glass vial, paperwork and a reel-to-reel recorder animate into view.
scenes.narration: So what were all these subprojects actually doing? The director sorted them into categories. Drugs and alcohol. Hypnosis. Sleep research. Polygraphs. The record also covers drugs meant as aids to interrogation. LSD was among the drugs tested. And here is the part that matters most. Some of the people tested were volunteers. Some were never told.

en.text: OK, what were they actually DOING?

en.caption: Think about that: some of them never knew.

scenes.title: The Human Cost
scenes.summary: Evidence of testing without informed consent. The room turns quiet and serious.
scenes.narration: The testimony counted six subprojects that tested drugs on unwitting people. Unwitting means they didn't know. Some of those tests happened in safe houses in San Francisco and New York City. There was no informed consent. One case shows what that meant. Dr. Frank Olson was an Army civilian employee. In 1953, at a meeting called by the CIA, he was given LSD without knowing it. About a week later, he was dead.

en.label: 6 OF 149 SUBPROJECTS

scenes.title: The Revelation
scenes.summary: Committee and hearing papers fill an evidence board. Agent Fox points to the records.
scenes.narration: So how did any of this come out? In January 1975, the Senate created a special committee, chaired by Senator Frank Church. Its job was to find out whether America's intelligence agencies had done anything illegal, improper or unethical. Then, in 1977, a CIA employee found seven boxes of MKUltra records at a retired records center. That August, senators questioned the CIA director at a joint hearing. Senator Edward Kennedy said the CIA had drugged American citizens without their knowledge or consent.

en.text: So how did the secret get out?
The CIA drugged American citizens without their knowledge or consent.

scenes.title: What We Know
scenes.summary: The room brightens. Agent Fox closes the folder and a source-based takeaway appears.
scenes.narration: But those boxes were never the full story. A 1963 report by the CIA's Inspector General led to the end of unwitting testing in 1964. And in 1973, MKUltra files were destroyed on the authority of the CIA director at the time. Senator Kennedy named him: Richard Helms. What survived was mostly finance folders. Advances, vouchers, accountings. So what do we actually know? Enough to show it happened. Not enough to know everything that happened. Much of the full story may never be known.
